name: Yolŋu religion (Wangarr)

dating.dating_summary: Regional human occupation of Arnhem Land (Madjedbebe, contested ~65,000 BP) is evidence about the region, not about any specific Yolŋu ceremonial content; the earliest outsider documentation of Yolŋu religious practice specifically is Lloyd Warner's 1926-29 fieldwork, published 1937; the tradition's own internal claim is explicitly atemporal (Wangarr is not "in the past" in a linear sense); no independently verified oral-transmission-depth estimate exists for this tradition's specific narrative content.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Madjedbebe rock shelter optical dating: Clarkson et al., "Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago," Nature 547 (2017): 306-310, proposes ~65,000 BP; contested on sediment-taphonomy grounds against earlier ~50,000-60,000 BP thermoluminescence dates (Roberts, Jones & Smith, 1990). DISPUTED, and in any case this dates regional human presence, NOT any specific Yolŋu ceremony or narrative — do not conflate.

earliest_written_attestation.note: W. Lloyd Warner, A Black Civilization: A Social Study of an Australian Tribe (New York: Harper, 1937), from fieldwork 1926-29 (under Warner's "Murngin" terminology, now superseded).

surviving_manuscript_date.note: No manuscript tradition; systematized in later academic ethnography — Ronald and Catherine Berndt (1946-47, 1949-50 fieldwork), Ian Keen, Knowledge and Secrecy in an Aboriginal Religion (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994), and Howard Morphy, Ancestral Connections (University of Chicago Press, 1991).

tradition_internal_claim.note: Wangarr denotes both the ancestral beings and an ancestral era that is not confined to "the past" but continues to structure the present — internally resists linear-date framing by its own logic.

estimated_oral_origin.method: No scholar has applied Nunn and Reid's oral-tradition/sea-level-correlation dating method (Australian Geographer 47(1), 2016) to the Wagilag/Wawilak narrative specifically. Regional western-Arnhem-Land rock-art dating of Rainbow-Serpent-type imagery to ~6,000-8,000 BP (Taçon, Wilson & Chippindale, Archaeology in Oceania 31(3), 1996) is geographically and culturally distinct Bininj/Mungguy material, not Yolŋu, and must not be used as a proxy date.

notes: Structuring principle: Dhuwa and Yirritja, exogamous patrilineal moieties dividing the entire cosmos (clans, languages, land, water, celestial phenomena) — nothing is moiety-neutral. Terms: Wangarr (ancestral beings/era), märr (spiritual power in land, a Yolŋu analogue to Pacific "mana" — Bentley James, in Strings of Connectedness, ANU Press, 2015), madayin (customary law, used in the Milirrpum judgment). Note on Stanner's "The Dreaming": his foundational essay (Australian Signpost, ed. Hungerford, Melbourne: F.W. Cheshire, 1956, pp. 51-65 — not 1953/Traditional Aboriginal Society as sometimes cited) drew on his own Murinbata (Daly River) fieldwork, NOT Yolŋu material — the "Dreaming" gloss now conventionally applied to Wangarr is a later interpretive overlay from a different region's ethnography, not an original Yolŋu-sourced concept. See claim_jukurrpa_terminology_and_dreaming_gloss_critique for the general critique of this gloss.
